title: Eclipses: Shadows in Space
summary: How the Sun and Moon line up to cast shadows, and why eclipses do not happen every month.

steps.title: A shadow game
sentences: An eclipse happens when one space object moves into the shadow of another.
Earth, the Moon and the Sun are the three players.
There are two kinds that we see from Earth: solar eclipses and lunar eclipses.

steps.title: Solar eclipse
sentences: In a solar eclipse the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth.
The Moon blocks the Sun's light and its shadow falls on a small part of Earth.
The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but also about 400 times farther away, so the Moon can just cover it.
points: The Moon's shadow falls on Earth
Sun and Moon look the same size

steps.title: Lunar eclipse
sentences: In a lunar eclipse, Earth is in the middle, and the Moon moves into Earth's shadow.
The Moon often looks dull red, because some sunlight bends through Earth's air and reaches it.
A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with the eyes, but a solar eclipse is not.

steps.title: Why not every month?
sentences: The Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees compared with Earth's orbit around the Sun.
So most months the Moon passes a little above or below the straight line.
An eclipse happens only when the three line up closely enough.
points: Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees

facts: Never look directly at the Sun, even during an eclipse, without proper eclipse glasses.
The darkest part of a solar eclipse is called totality and can last up to about seven minutes.
Ancient astronomers learned to predict eclipses by noticing repeating cycles.

quiz.q: In a solar eclipse, which object is in the middle?
quiz.why: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth.

quiz.q: Why do eclipses not happen every month?
quiz.why: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees, so it usually misses the shadow line.

quiz.q: Which eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes?
quiz.why: A lunar eclipse only dims reflected light, so it is safe. Looking at the Sun is never safe.
